A cyber-physical workcell for CAFI circuit breaker riveting and inspection

A collaborative robot, a two-fixture rotary table, a vision camera and a live digital twin, working together as one automated cell for the Schneider Electric challenge.

Team project, built with three classmates
Author
Diego Becerra Fuentes
Course
Automation of Manufacturing Systems, Tec de Monterrey
Delivered
June 2026

The part’s journey through the cell, from delivery to classification.

The problem

Riveting and inspecting a circuit-breaker part depends on where the part sits. When people place and check it by hand, the position drifts from cycle to cycle, defects slip through visual checks, and almost nothing is recorded.

Our challenge was to automate that one critical stage as a semi-automated cell, without building a full production line. Five rivets per part had to be positioned within 1 mm and verified on every piece, not by sampling.

Handle

A cobot and custom gripper move each CAFI from conveyor to fixture.

Rivet

A two-fixture rotary table lets one part rivet while the next one loads.

Inspect

A camera checks all five rivets and the cell sorts the part as OK or NOK.

Supervise

PLC, HMI, SCADA and a digital twin show what the cell is doing at every moment.

Specific objectives
  • Supply unriveted CAFI parts to the work area continuously and reliably.
  • Hold each part by its reference surfaces so riveting and inspection stay aligned.
  • Position five rivet points with repeatability below 1 mm.
  • Handle and transfer the part with a cobot and custom gripper, safely and consistently.
  • Verify presence and condition of all five rivets inline with vision, not by sampling.
  • Classify every part as OK or NOK and route it to its own bin.
  • Coordinate states, interlocks, counters, inspection results and resets from the control logic.
  • Give operators HMI and SCADA views of status, variables, alarms, cycle progress and results.
  • Validate the whole sequence in a digital twin before full physical implementation.
Step-by-step sequence
  1. A ramp feeds an unriveted CAFI onto the conveyor, and a photoelectric sensor stops the belt at the pickup point.
  2. The cobot closes the gripper on the part and places it in the first fixture on the rotary table. A limit switch confirms it is seated.
  3. The table indexes and the riveting state starts, represented by a 30 s timer.
  4. While the first part rivets, the cobot loads a second CAFI into the other fixture.
  5. After the timer, the table turns and the first part is moved to the separate inspection fixture.
  6. The camera checks the five rivets once the cobot has cleared its view.
  7. An OK part goes to the accepted bin; if any rivet fails, it goes to the rejected bin.

Digital twin

Before touching hardware, we modeled the cell twice. First the layout in AutoCAD, to check reach and clearances. Then the cobot and table in ROS as URDF models, to confirm every pick and place pose was reachable.

The validated model moved to a browser-based 3D twin built with React, TypeScript and Three.js. A finite state machine drives it, and a scheduler plus safety interlocks stop impossible moves, like turning the table while the cobot is still over it.

How the twin behaves

The rotary table holds two fixtures and turns 180 degrees between HOME and WORK, so one CAFI can wait or load while another is in the riveting position. That also let us measure waiting times and overlaps.

Finite state machine

It runs the sequence from conveyor detection through pick, placement, table indexing, riveting, transfer, camera verdict and bin delivery, and it rejects invalid states such as two parts in one resource.

Scheduler and interlocks

  • Priority goes to inspected parts, then riveted parts, then parts waiting to enter.
  • The table cannot turn while the cobot is in its zone or carrying a fresh part toward it.
  • No part goes to the camera while the inspection fixture is occupied.
  • Gripper, fixture and camera serve one part at a time.

Riveting itself is represented by a 30-second timer, so the twin and prototype validate sequence and timing rather than rivet force.

How the cell is built

Physical layer

Ramp and conveyor, cobot with pneumatic gripper, rotary table, inspection fixture and two output bins.

Control layer

A Raspberry Pi reads four limit switches and steps the NEMA 17 motor; the cobot controller reads two photoelectric sensors.

Monitoring layer

HMI and SCADA show states, counters, cycle times and alarms.

Digital layer

The twin mirrors the logic and timing of the real cell for safe testing.

Everything talks over one Ethernet switch, mostly Modbus TCP, with the Raspberry Pi as the gateway. That kept wiring small: no sensor is needed for every part position.

Signals, sensors and actuators
DeviceRoleConnected to
4 limit switchesTable end positions and fixture presenceRaspberry Pi
Photoelectric sensor 1Part at conveyor pickup, stops the beltCobot controller
Photoelectric sensor 2Part in inspection fixture, arms the cameraCobot controller
NEMA 17 stepperTurns the table (step and direction, 12 V driver)Raspberry Pi
2 pneumatic valvesOpen and close the gripper pistonCobot controller
Conveyor motorDelivers parts, with a protection diodeCobot controller

The camera is triggered only after the robot leaves its field of view, so the cobot never blocks the inspection.

Mechanical work

The rotary table is an MDF disk with two fixtures on opposite ends, carried on rollers and driven by a belt from a stepper motor. Limit switches mark both ends of travel and the presence of a part. We CNC-machined the inspection fixture in wood and 3D printed the rest. A custom PCB ties the switches, motor driver and Pi together.

Software stack

Python / FastAPI gatewayModbus TCPREST + WebSocket, 100 ms telemetryCORBA vision triggerModicon M262 PLCDatalogic P15 cameraReact / TypeScript / Three.js

The Pi runs a pipeline manager that schedules both fixtures, times the rivet dwell, triggers the camera and routes each part to the right bin. An encrypted tunnel lets the twin run from any network.

Gateway, PLC, vision and cobot programming

Raspberry Pi gateway

A Raspberry Pi 4 bridges the cobot (TLS/JSON), the PLC and HMI (Modbus TCP) and the camera (CORBA), and exposes one REST and WebSocket API to every client.

PLC

The Modicon M262, programmed in EcoStruxure Machine Expert, conditions I/O: photoeye, presence sensors, table limits and e-stop in; conveyor relay, rivet dwell signal, stack light and camera trigger out. It does not run robot motion.

Vision

A Datalogic P15 looks down on the fixture, where all five rivet points are exposed. A calibrated pattern-matching job finds the rivet markers, and lighting and shutter can be tuned remotely. The OK/NOK result feeds the HMI and the bin-routing logic.

Cobot and gripper

The cobot moves between preset poses (32 joint-space poses in the final calibration). The gripper has one fixed jaw and one piston-driven jaw, both with flexible pads. It opens with the fixed jaw almost touching the part so closing does not shake it.

SCADA and HMI

The SCADA is a browser dashboard with a Real mode, streaming from the cell, and a Simulation mode that replays the same pipeline without hardware. It speaks six languages and gives operators, engineers and admins different views.

Beyond counters and alarms, it adds four analytic panels: operator guidance, predictive maintenance, process optimization and anomaly detection.

Monitored variables
  • System state, cobot task, fixture occupancy, table position (HOME, WORK or moving)
  • Riveting timer, camera status and inspection verdict
  • OK and NOK counters, current, last and average cycle time, waiting times
  • Alarms and communication status (REAL, STALE or NOT CONNECTED)
  • Cobot health: power, e-stop, per-joint current and temperature, TCP pose, error codes
  • 14 digital I/O signals, gripper state and air pressure
The four analytic panels
  • Operator guidance: the current decision (continue, pause, stop) with a recovery procedure and a logged confirmation.
  • Predictive maintenance: remaining useful life of the riveting tool, cycle count, load and vibration trends.
  • Process optimization: throughput, idle time, energy per cycle and suggested speed, delay and timing setpoints.
  • Anomaly detection: z-score outliers and safety flags such as e-stop and collision.

Results

All eight validation tests passed: delivery, cobot handling, two-fixture table, riveting timer, vision inspection, classification, SCADA/HMI and the twin. The real run, though, exposed the true bottleneck. The cobot was idle 80.8% of the time, mostly waiting and travelling to far safe positions.

Average cycle time

Real run181.9 s
Optimized simulation138.8 s

Cobot idle time

Real run80.8%
Optimized simulation22.0%

We used the twin to fix it: skipping needless returns to safe positions, adding a short clearance pose so the table can turn sooner, adding high transition poses to avoid collisions, and delivering inspected parts before moving a new one to the camera.

MetricBeforeOptimizedGain
CAFI 1 cycle120.0 s104.4 s15.6 s faster
CAFI 2 cycle210.5 s147.2 s63.3 s faster
CAFI 3 cycle204.0 s160.2 s43.8 s faster
CAFI 4 cycle147.2 s143.3 s3.9 s faster
Average cycle181.9 s138.8 s43.1 s faster
Cobot idle80.8%22.0%58.8 points lower
Validation results, test by test
TestWhat we sawStatus
CAFI deliveryConveyor delivered and sensor stopped the belt at pickupPass
Cobot handlingPick, transfer and placement validatedPass
Rotating fixtureTwo parts held at once, one riveting while one waitsPass
Riveting simulation30 s state ran before the process could continuePass
Vision inspectionFive rivets evaluated in the inspection fixturePass

SCADA and HMIState, task, verdict, counters and cycle data shownPass
Digital twinFull sequence represented, logic and visualsPass
The optimization, in detail
  • Removed automatic returns to SAFE_RETURN, SAFE_RIVET and SAFE_CAMERA; the cobot now checks the next available task and goes straight to it.
  • Added a short clearance pose, LIFT_PLACE_FIXTURE_CLEAR, so the table can rotate once the cobot is lifted clear.
  • Added high transition poses (APPROACH_FIXTURE_HIGH, APPROACH_CAMERA_HIGH, LIFT_PLACE_CAMERA_HIGH, CAMERA_TO_CONVEYOR_CLEAR) so long moves do not cross the table.
  • Changed scheduler priority so inspected parts are delivered before a new part goes to the camera.
  • Used measured timings: 5 s inspection, 30 s riveting and real segment times for cobot and table.

One honest limit: riveting was simulated, so we validated control, timing and monitoring, not rivet force or tooling durability.

From plan to working cell

We were given a Lexium cobot, a PLC, an HMI and a camera. We planned the sequence first (receive, rivet, inspect, deliver), then designed fixtures around it. The first idea was wood for every fixture; for simplicity we machined only the inspection one and 3D printed the others. Seeing that two parts could be processed at once led to the rotary base.

Mechanical

Rotary table, conveyor, inspection fixture and bins aligned and checked for repeatability across many robot cycles.

Robotic

32 poses calibrated to the real layout, and a two-slot pipeline tuned to remove fixture conflicts.

Control

The Raspberry Pi confirmed as the main controller, with the HMI following cell state in under 100 ms.

Monitoring

The encrypted tunnel held continuous streaming, and the twin worked from outside the local network.

Digital

SCADA panels, HMI twin, tracking windows and languages re-tested after each hardware milestone.

The HMI panel, a Harmony HMIST6400, was programmed from the Raspberry Pi using a reverse-engineered upload protocol for Operator Terminal Expert, with live I/O, counters and command buttons over Modbus. A parallel simulation mode let us validate sequences, PASS/FAIL routing and counter accuracy without hardware, and the same telemetry feeds both modes.

CAD and hardware gallery

What comes next

Mechanics

Stiffer fixtures and table, plus a faster, safer indexing mechanism.

Sensing

A conveyor camera so the cobot adapts its pick pose to each part.

Vision

Better lighting and calibration, and image logging for traceability.

Industry

Real riveting tests, formal safety validation and MES integration.

Limitations and further ideas
  • Riveting was simulated, so force, deformation and tooling life are untested.
  • Sensing and vision reliability under changing light need more work, along with fixture rigidity and network error handling.
  • A faster table must be paired with safety validation.
  • Industrial use would add production data logging, preventive maintenance indicators and a link to a plant database or MES.

Conclusion

This project joined mechanical design, robotics, control, vision and software in one working system. The digital twin did more than demonstrate it: it let us find the bottleneck, test fixes safely and cut cycle time by almost a quarter before changing the physical cell.

It was a team effort across all those areas, and the first time I worked on a cell where so many subsystems had to stay in sync. With sturdier fixtures and real riveting tests, it could grow into a full Industry 4.0 station.
